migrationNotes: Spine: two office remarks about the milk look alike on the page, and the lesson teaches one test that separates them: try to break the argument by building a situation where the premises hold and the conclusion fails. The hunt starts as a story, becomes a table of rows, grows to three letters, and ends by separating an argument that cannot fail from one that is also true to the facts.

lesson.title: Valid, sound and counterexamples

lead.text: Start with Dev's remark and test it. Suppose the rule on the note holds and Ruth did use the last of the milk. Try to describe a situation in which she did not buy more. You will find that you can't, because the rule forbids it. Once the premises are granted, the conclusion cannot be false.

An argument like that is called valid. Validity is about the link between the premises and the conclusion, and you judge it by trying to break the link: looking for a possible situation in which every premise is true and the conclusion is false. Such a situation is a counterexample, and an argument that has one is invalid. The figure sets each remark against a possible situation, and its buttons switch between Dev's remark and Sam's.

afterFigure.text: Now try the same on Sam's. The rule holds and Ruth did bring in a carton, yet it is easy to describe a situation where the conclusion fails: someone else used the last of the office milk, and Ruth bought a carton because her own fridge at home was empty. Both premises are true and the conclusion is false, so the argument is invalid.

One counterexample is enough. You don't have to show that the situation really happened, only that it could, with the premises true and the conclusion false. That is why testing an argument is a search. You are hunting for a single case that breaks it, and you are allowed to make the case up.

steps.headline: Checking every case with a table

lead.text: Hunting for a counterexample by imagination works for small cases, but it depends on your thinking of the right situation. A table makes sure you have looked everywhere. Replace each simple claim in the argument with a letter, then list every combination of true and false for those letters.

Take the pavement again, this time with the second premise changed: “If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet. It rained overnight. So the pavement is wet.” Let p stand for “it rained overnight” and q for “the pavement is wet”. Claims like these, with no smaller sentences inside them, are called atomic sentences. With the letters in place the argument is reduced to its form: p → q, p, so q. The arrow reads “if p then q”, and p → q is false only when p is true and q is false, like a promise that is broken only when the condition holds and the result doesn't follow.

Two atomic sentences can be true or false in four combinations. Write them all out, with the premises and the conclusion worked out for each. That list is called a truth table. Each combination is a row, and a row describes one possible situation.

afterFigure.text: Read the first case. Only one row makes both premises true: p true and q true. The conclusion q is true in that row too, so no row has true premises and a false conclusion. There is no counterexample, and the argument is valid. Step through the second case's rows to see which one breaks it.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
It rained overnight.
If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
It did not rain overnight.

lead.text: The table settles validity, and the reason has to do with what a counterexample is.

Now the pavement argument you judged earlier, written in letters: p → q, q, so p. List its four rows, by hand or by stepping through them in the figure, and count the ones where both premises are true.

reveal.text: You counted by hand: two rows keep both premises true, and in one of them p is false while q is true. That row is the counterexample, the night when something other than rain wet the pavement.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
The pavement is wet.
If the lamp is plugged in, the room is lit.
The room is lit.

lead.text: The table gave the same verdict whatever p and q stand for. Rain and pavements, milk and offices: the letters stand for any of them. That means validity belongs to the pattern of an argument, its form, and a form that passes the table passes for every argument that fits it.

A few forms are common enough to have names. “If p then q; p; so q” is modus ponens, which the table showed to be valid. “If p then q; q; so p” is affirming the consequent, the pattern behind Sam's remark about the milk and the wet pavement, and the table showed it to be invalid. A third valid form is “p or q; not p; so q”, called disjunctive syllogism: if one of two options is ruled out, the other remains.

afterFigure.text: Knowing the names lets you recognise a form on sight, but the table stays in charge. When a form is new to you, build the table or hunt for a counterexample, and don't rely on a name or a feeling that it looks right. Some invalid forms feel very convincing, and the next lesson looks at several of them.

lead.text: Real arguments rarely stop at two atomic sentences. Each extra letter doubles the number of rows, because every existing row splits into one where the new letter is true and one where it is false. Two letters give four rows, three give eight and four give sixteen. By ten letters there are more than a thousand.

That is fine for a short argument and tedious for a long one, so it pays to search with some direction. Start from the conclusion. A conclusion of the form p → r is false only in the rows where p is true and r is false. Fix those two values, then ask what each premise needs from the remaining letter q. If no value of q keeps every premise true, there is no counterexample. If some value does, you have found one.

afterFigure.text: Work it through for the chain in the figure's first case. The conclusion p → r is false only when p is true and r is false, which leaves two rows, one with q true and one with q false. In the first, the second premise q → r fails, since q is true and r is false. In the second, the first premise p → q fails. Neither row keeps both premises true, so the chain is valid. You checked two rows instead of eight. The second case tries the same search on a conclusion that goes the other way.

steps.headline: Valid is not the same as true

lead.text: So far you have asked only whether the conclusion would have to be true if the premises were. You haven't asked whether the premises are true. Compare two arguments. “All mammals breathe air; whales are mammals; so whales breathe air.” “All cats are reptiles; Whiskers is a cat; so Whiskers is a reptile.” Both are valid, because in each case true premises would force the conclusion.

The difference is in the premises. Everything in the first argument is true. The second begins with a falsehood, so its conclusion is false even though nothing is wrong with the reasoning. A valid argument whose premises are all true is called sound. A valid argument with a false premise, like the cats, is unsound, and it gives you no guarantee that its conclusion is true. The figure sets out the four combinations of valid or invalid with true or false premises, then places these examples in it.

afterFigure.text: Soundness is what you want from an argument, and validity is the half that logic can check by itself. The other half is a matter of checking facts. One consequence is worth holding on to: if an argument is valid and its conclusion is false, at least one premise must be false, since true premises would have forced a true conclusion. So when a valid argument has a conclusion you can't accept, look at its premises.

premises.text: All mammals breathe air.
Whales are mammals.
All cats are reptiles.
Whiskers is a cat.

lead.text: This argument is valid, so any fault lies in its premises. Check each premise against what you know about metals.

lesson.orientation: Test validity by searching for a counterexample row, and separate a valid argument from a sound one.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The office kitchen has a note by the fridge: whoever uses the last of the milk buys more. One morning Dev says, “Ruth used the last of the milk yesterday, so she'll have bought some more.” Nobody argues. Later Sam says, “Ruth came in with a carton this afternoon, so she must be the one who used the last of it.” This time people frown, although the two remarks look alike on the page. Each puts the rule beside a fact and draws a conclusion.

Dev's remark leaves no way out. If the rule holds and Ruth used the last of the milk, she bought more, whatever else was going on. Sam's remark leaves a gap, because Ruth could have bought milk for her own kitchen. The two look the same until you test them, and spotting the gap quickly and exactly is a skill.
Last lesson you learned to lay an argument out. This lesson asks how firmly its premises hold up its conclusion, and it gives you a test you can run on any argument, in your head or on paper.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test an argument by trying to break it and explain why an unbreakable one can still have a false conclusion.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is valid when no possible situation makes every premise true and the conclusion false. It is sound when it is also valid and every premise is true.

blocks.text: You hunted for counterexamples to Sam's remark about the milk and to the wet pavement, settled a form by listing its rows, shortened an eight-row search by starting from the conclusion, and saw that a valid argument can still have a false premise.

recap.nextHook: Some arguments look valid when they are not, and others hide a flaw in a word or a choice of options. The next lesson names the commonest of these slips and shows how to answer an argument at its strongest.

questions.prompt: Premises: 'If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet' and 'The pavement is wet'. Conclusion: 'It rained overnight'. Is the argument valid or invalid?
hints: Look for a possible situation in which both premises are true and the conclusion is false.
Could the pavement be wet for some other reason?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Invalid: a burst water main on a dry night makes both premises true and the conclusion false.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid: wet pavement has other causes, so the premises can be true with a false conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for another way the pavement could be wet. If there is one, the premises do not force the conclusion.

questions.prompt: For the form 'p → q, q, so p', in how many of the four truth-table rows are both premises true?
hints: List the four rows: TT, TF, FT, FF for p and q.
The second premise, q, removes every row where q is false.
Check p → q in the rows that remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both premises are true when p and q are both true, and when p is false and q true. In the second of those rows the conclusion is false.

questions.onCorrect: Two rows keep both premises true, and in one of them the conclusion is false.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every row. The second premise rules some out.
Check the row with p false and q true. Are both premises true there?

questions.prompt: In 'All metals are magnetic; copper is a metal; so copper is magnetic', which premise is false? Answer with its number, 1 or 2.
hints: Validity is not in question here; check each premise against the facts.
Does a fridge magnet stick to a copper pipe?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Premise 1 is false: copper is a metal but is not attracted by a magnet. The argument is valid and unsound.

questions.onCorrect: Premise 1 is false, and the argument is still valid. Validity does not depend on the facts.

misconceptions.feedback: Copper is a metal, which is all premise 2 says. Check the other premise against the facts.

questions.prompt: How many of the eight truth-table rows are counterexamples to 'p → q, r → q, so p → r'?
hints: Start from the conclusion: when is p → r false?
In those rows, which value of q makes the first premise true?
Check the second premise in the row that remains.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The conclusion is false only when p is true and r false. Then p → q needs q true, and r → q is true because r is false. One row: p true, q true, r false.

questions.onCorrect: One row: p and q true, r false. That single counterexample shows the form invalid.

misconceptions.feedback: The conclusion fails when p is true and r false. Check whether both premises survive there.
Fix p true and r false. Only one value of q can then keep the first premise true.

questions.prompt: A valid argument has a false conclusion. What must be the case?
hints: Suppose every premise were true. What would validity then require?

acceptedIdeas: At least one premise is false
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If every premise were true, validity would force a true conclusion. So at least one premise is false, though not necessarily all.

choices.label: At least one premise is false
The argument is not valid after all

questions.onCorrect: At least one premise must be false. If all were true, validity would force a true conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: Only one false premise is needed. The others may be true.
The argument is stated to be valid. Ask what validity requires if the conclusion is false.

questions.prompt: A complete truth table for an argument with four different atomic sentences has how many rows?
hints: One atomic sentence gives two rows, true and false.
Each new atomic sentence doubles the number of rows.
Calculate 2 raised to the power of the number of atomic sentences.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each atomic sentence doubles the rows: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

questions.onCorrect: Each atomic sentence doubles the rows: four sentences give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the table for three atomic sentences. A fourth doubles it again.
That is how many sentences there are. Each one doubles the rows.

questions.prompt: At a party every guest was given a badge. Priya was a guest. Could both of those claims be true and yet Priya not have been given a badge? Answer yes or no.
hints: Picture Priya at the party. What was true of every guest?
To answer yes you would have to describe the party where both claims hold and Priya has no badge.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. If every guest got a badge and Priya was a guest, she got one.

questions.onCorrect: No gap is possible. When the claims are true, the conclusion is forced. That is the idea behind validity.

misconceptions.feedback: Try to picture it. Priya is a guest, and every guest was given a badge. Where would the gap be?

questions.prompt: What shows that an argument is invalid?
hints: Think of what validity rules out.

acceptedIdeas: A possible situation with true premises and a false conclusion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A possible situation with true premises and a false conclusion

choices.label: A possible situation with true premises and a false conclusion

questions.onCorrect: A counterexample is exactly that situation. One is enough to show invalidity.

misconceptions.feedback: Valid arguments can have false premises. Invalidity needs a situation where the premises are true and the conclusion false.
Surprise is a feeling. Validity is about whether the premises can all hold while the conclusion fails.

questions.prompt: Why does checking every row of the truth table settle whether an argument form is valid?
hints: A counterexample must be one of the rows.

acceptedIdeas: It covers every way the premises could come out true.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It covers every way the premises could come out true.

choices.label: It covers every way the premises could come out true.
It checks whether the premises are true in real life.
It tests only the most likely row.

questions.onCorrect: A counterexample would have to appear among the rows, so a complete table settles validity.

misconceptions.feedback: The rows are possibilities, not facts. Validity does not depend on what is actually the case.
Every row counts, including unlikely ones. A single bad row is enough.

questions.prompt: “All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly.” Is this argument valid? Answer yes or no.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. If both premises were true, the conclusion would have to be. The first premise is false, so it is unsound.

questions.onCorrect: Valid: true premises would force the conclusion. The false first premise makes it unsound.

misconceptions.feedback: Validity ignores whether the premises are true. Suppose both were true: would the conclusion have to be?
